lead: A radiation pattern is a shape: field or power plotted against direction. A link budget cannot use a whole shape, so the shape is reduced to a few numbers. Directivity says how strongly the antenna favours its best direction compared with an isotropic radiator. Gain is directivity reduced by the antenna’s own losses. Beamwidth says how wide the main beam is. This chapter defines radiation intensity, beam solid angle, directivity, gain, half-power and first-null beamwidths, and shows how they are quoted in dBi on a datasheet.
prereq: You need: the far field of the Hertzian dipole and its sin θ pattern (Hertzian dipole).

sections.h3: The radiation pattern and its lobes

blocks.text: Measure the far field on a large sphere round the antenna and plot it against the angles θ (from the antenna axis) and φ (round the axis). A field pattern plots |E| normalised to its peak, a power pattern plots |E|², and a dB pattern plots the power pattern in decibels (peak 0 dB, half power −3 dB). Two cuts through the peak are used: the E-plane, containing the electric field, and the H-plane, containing the magnetic field. For a vertical dipole these are any vertical plane and the horizontal plane.

The pattern breaks into lobes separated by nulls, directions where the field falls to zero. The main lobe is the lobe that contains the direction of maximum radiation. Every other lobe is a minor lobe; those beside the main lobe are side lobes, and the one pointing opposite the main lobe is the back lobe. The side-lobe level is the peak of the largest side lobe in dB below the main peak, and the front-to-back ratio compares the main peak with the back lobe.

An isotropic radiator (equal in all directions) is only a reference; an omnidirectional antenna is uniform in one plane, like a dipole; a directional antenna, like a dish, puts most of its power into one main lobe.

sections.h3: Radiation intensity, beam solid angle and directivity

blocks.text: In the far field the power density S (W/m²) falls as 1/r². Multiplying by r² removes the spreading and leaves a quantity that depends only on direction, the radiation intensity U = r² S, in watts per steradian (W/sr). The total radiated power is its integral over the sphere, Prad = ∯ U dΩ, where dΩ = sin θ dθ dφ is the element of solid angle and the whole sphere is 4π sr.
D = 4π Umax / Prad = 4π / ΩA. D is the directivity, a plain ratio; Umax is the peak intensity; ΩA is the beam solid angle in sr

The beam solid angle ΩA = ∯ Pn dΩ, with Pn = U/Umax the normalised power pattern, is the solid angle the power would fill if it flowed at peak intensity everywhere inside it and nowhere else. An isotropic source has Pn = 1 everywhere, ΩA = 4π and D = 1. Squeeze the beam and D grows. In decibels, D(dBi) = 10 log₁₀ D, “i” for isotropic.
G = ηrad D. G is the gain; ηrad is the radiation efficiency, the fraction of the power accepted at the terminals that is radiated (0 to 1)

Losses heat the metal and dielectric without changing the pattern, so they lower G and leave D alone: G = D only for a lossless antenna. Gain is the number a link budget uses, quoted in dBi, or in dBd relative to a half-wave dipole (dBd = dBi − 2.15).

The half-power beamwidth (HPBW) is the angle between the two directions in the main lobe where the power pattern is half its peak (−3 dB), which is where the field pattern is 1/√2 = 0.707 of its peak. The first-null beamwidth (FNBW) is the angle between the first nulls either side of the main lobe; it is always wider than the HPBW.

For a single narrow pencil beam a quick estimate links beamwidth to directivity: D ≈ 41 253 / (θE θH), where θE and θH are the half-power beamwidths in the E-plane and the H-plane, in degrees, and 41 253 is the number of square degrees in a sphere (4π × (180/π)²). It treats the beam as flat-topped and ignores side lobes, so it is rough for broad beams and wrong for more than one major lobe.
Datasheets also give the input match as return loss, −20 log₁₀|Γ| dB, or as VSWR (see reflection coefficient, standing waves and VSWR).

figure.caption: The two worked examples drawn as power patterns. Both have a 90° half-power beamwidth, yet the second puts all its power into the upper half space, so its directivity is 6.00 (7.78 dBi) against the dipole’s 1.5 (1.76 dBi).

spec.aria: Left: the power pattern sine squared theta of a short dipole, two lobes either side of a vertical axis, with half-power points at 45 and 135 degrees and a 90 degree beamwidth arc; directivity 1.5. Right: a single upward lobe cos squared theta above a ground line, half-power points at 45 degrees either side of vertical, beamwidth 90 degrees, directivity 6.

examples.question: An antenna has the field pattern F(θ) = sin θ with no φ dependence (the Hertzian dipole). Find its HPBW, beam solid angle and directivity, and its gain in dBi if η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.9.
steps: Power pattern: P<sub>n</sub> = F² = sin²θ. Half power where sin²θ = 0.5, so sin θ = 0.7071 and θ = 45° or 135°.
Ω<sub>A</sub> = ∫∫ sin²θ sin θ dθ dφ = 2π × (integral of sin³θ from 0 to π) = 2π × 4/3 = 8.378 sr.
G = η<sub>rad</sub> D = 0.9 × 1.5 = 1.35, that is 10 log₁₀ 1.35 = 1.30 dBi.

examples.question: A patch-like antenna radiates only into the upper half space with radiation intensity U = U₀ cos²θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 90° and U = 0 below. Find (a) its exact directivity, (b) its HPBW, (c) the estimate 41 253/(θ<sub>E</sub> θ<sub>H</sub>) and its error in dB, and (d) its gain in dBi if η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.8.
steps: P<sub>rad</sub> = ∫ from 0 to 2π ∫ from 0 to π/2 of U₀ cos²θ sin θ dθ dφ = 2π U₀ × 1/3 = 2.094 U₀.
D = 4π U<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>rad</sub> = 4π U₀ / (2.094 U₀) = 6.00, that is 7.78 dBi.
Half power: cos²θ = 0.5 gives θ = 45° either side of the axis, so HPBW = 90° in every plane through the axis: θ<sub>E</sub> = θ<sub>H</sub> = 90°.
The estimate is low by 7.78 − 7.07 = 0.71 dB, because this beam is broad and not flat-topped.
examples.answer: D = 6.00 (7.78 dBi); HPBW = 90°; the beamwidth estimate gives 5.09 (7.07 dBi), 0.71 dB low; G = 4.80 (6.81 dBi).

traps: Taking half power where the field is 0.5. Half power is where the field is 0.707 (power 0.5); field 0.5 is the −6 dB point.
Using D ≈ 41 253/(θ<sub>E</sub> θ<sub>H</sub>) with angles in radians, or for a broad or multi-lobe beam. It needs degrees and one pencil beam, and even then it is an estimate.
Writing G > D. Gain is directivity times an efficiency of at most 1, so G ≤ D; “lossless” in a question means G = D.
Adding dBi values to plain ratios. Convert first: 3 dBi is a ratio of 2, not 3, and G = η<sub>rad</sub> D is done in ratios, then converted.
Calling the back lobe “all the minor lobes”. Minor lobes are every lobe except the main one; the back lobe is only the one opposite the main beam.

quiz.q: Define directivity and give its value for an isotropic radiator.
quiz.a: D = 4πU<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>rad</sub> = 4π/Ω<sub>A</sub>, the peak intensity over the average intensity. An isotropic radiator has D = 1 (0 dBi).

quiz.q: What are the E-plane and H-plane patterns?
quiz.a: Pattern cuts through the direction of maximum radiation: the E-plane contains the electric field vector, the H-plane contains the magnetic field vector.

quiz.q: Why can gain never exceed directivity?
quiz.a: G = η<sub>rad</sub> D with η<sub>rad</sub> ≤ 1. Losses reduce the radiated power but not the pattern shape, so they can only lower the gain.

quiz.q: State the difference between HPBW and FNBW.
quiz.a: HPBW is the angle between the −3 dB points of the main lobe; FNBW is the angle between the first nulls either side of it. FNBW is always the wider.

quiz.q: A pencil beam has θ<sub>E</sub> = 10° and θ<sub>H</sub> = 20°. Estimate D in dBi, and the gain if η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.7.
A pattern has two equal main lobes, and the HPBW of one lobe is quoted. Can D ≈ 41 253/(θ<sub>E</sub> θ<sub>H</sub>) be used? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The estimate assumes all the power is in one pencil beam. Two equal lobes hold twice the solid angle, so the estimate from one lobe would be about twice too high; integrate the whole pattern and use D = 4π/Ω<sub>A</sub>.

quiz.q: Antenna A has D = 10 and η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.5; antenna B has D = 6 and η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.95. Which delivers the stronger signal in its best direction for the same input power?
quiz.a: G<sub>A</sub> = 5.0 (6.99 dBi), G<sub>B</sub> = 5.7 (7.56 dBi). B wins by 0.57 dB: gain, not directivity, sets the radiated field.

beyond: Not for the exam. Patterns are measured in anechoic chambers and simulated before hardware exists; 5G base stations and radars steer their main lobe electronically, so HPBW and side-lobe level become system numbers set in software. Search next for “realized gain” and “beamforming side-lobe level”.
